title: Tammy Fine to Lead Talent Development at NBC News
description: Tammy Fine, a veteran NBC News producer who spent a significant part of her career overseeing key newsmaker interviews in the first hour of “Today,”
body:
Tammy Fine, a veteran NBC News producer who spent a significant part of her career overseeing key newsmaker interviews in the first hour of “Today,” is getting a new passel of responsibilities.

	Fine has been named vice president of talent development at NBC News, and will lead efforts to develop careers and find up and coming journalists who might join the overall team. Liza Eaton, who has led that function, will move to a part-time role later this summer, and will report to FIne going forward.
	

	The announcement was made Tuesday in a memo from Rebecca Blumenstein, president of NBC News Editorial; Cheryl Rosenbloom, executive vice president of global human resources of NBCUniversal News Group; and Libby Leist, the executive vice president of “Today” and lifestyle programming. 


	Fine will begin her new duties on September 1.

	The executive started with NBC News as an intern on “NBC Nightly News” in 1993. She worked with then-anchor Tom Brokaw and subsequently joined “Today,” rising to a senior producer role. During her tenure, Fine has supervised interviews with every living U.S. president.  Her duties at NBC News had her covering the funerals of both Princess Diana and Mother Teresa, and traveling to Cuba, India, Israel, Hong Kong and Vietnam. She has also worked at MSNBC and served as an adjunct professor at Columbia University, where she taught a graduate course on strategic communication in the digital age.

	Kristen Powers, who joined as a talent-development executive earlier this year, will report to both Fine and to Catherine Kim, executive vice president of editorial for NBC News.

schema.headline: Tammy Fine to Lead Talent Development at NBC News

title: Goya-Nominated Zoe Bonafonte Leads Spain-Argentina Soccer Pioneer Drama ‘Veleta’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Goya-nominated actress Zoe Bonafonte (“El 47”) will play Spain’s first female soccer player, Ana “Nita” Carmona Ruiz, in “Veleta,” a Spain-Argentina
body:
Goya-nominated actress Zoe Bonafonte (“El 47”) will play Spain’s first female soccer player, Ana “Nita” Carmona Ruiz, in “Veleta,” a Spain-Argentina co-production directed and co-written by Paco Torres (“The Magic of Hope”) and now shooting in Andalusia.

	Goya winner Dani Rovira and “Vikings” actor Moe Dunford also star. Amaya Muruzábal, creator of “Hernán” and showrunner of Prime Video hit “Red Queen,” co-wrote and produces “Veleta.”
	

	Blend Studios, Muruzábal’s M Content, Nephilim Producciones and Buenos Aires-based Lahaye Media produce. Andalusia’s public broadcaster RTVA is also providing production funding.


	Set in early 20th-century Málaga, “Veleta” follows Carmona, a young working-class player determined to compete in a sport closed to women. She binds her chest, hides her hair and assumes the identity of “Veleta” to get onto the pitch, while her teammates keep her secret for decades.



	

									Zoe Bonafonte, Paco Torres & Javier Morgade © Raúl Pérez
	



	Bonafonte earned a best new actress Goya nomination for Marcel Barrena’s five-time Goya-winning “El 47.” Rovira, who won the 2015 Goya for best new actor for box-office smash “Spanish Affair,” plays Carmona’s father.

	The ensemble also includes Javier Morgade (“Our Fault”), Martin Urrutia (“Mariliendre”), Blanca Fernández, making her screen debut, Goya winner Adelfa Calvo (“The Motive”), Mariola Fuentes (“Broken Embraces”) and Eric Masip (“Through My Window”).



	

									Mariola Fuentes & Dani Rovira © Raúl Pérez
	



	The story begins in Málaga in 1917, as the city’s faeneras — fisherwomen — take to the streets and young men from working-class families are drawn into the Rif War.
	

	Shooting began in July across Málaga, Torrox, Antequera and Motril and is due to wrap in mid-August. The film is slated for release in 2027.

	“Our goal is to make a film that moves audiences, mobilizes them, and brings to light the largely unknown story of Anita Carmona,” Torres said, describing the project as “a tribute to Andalusia, to its color, its joy and its people.”

	“Nita didn’t just fight to play football: she fought to decide who she wanted to be, at a time when many women were denied that possibility,” he added.

	“There are women who blazed a trail long before the world was ready to recognize them. Nita was one of them,” said Marta Rangel, Blend Studios’ general manager and executive producer. “’Veleta’ also stems from the need to look back, reclaim those stories, and understand that many of the freedoms we enjoy today began with women who refused to accept the place they had been assigned.”

	Run by Luis Collar and Jorge Moreno, Nephilim’s credits include Daniel Hendler’s Venice-selected “A Loose End,” Manuel Martín Cuenca’s “Andrea’s Love” and Gracia Querejeta’s “Invisibles.”

	Lahaye Media combines production with a sizeable post-production operation, having worked on nearly 300 audiovisual productions, including titles for Disney+, Prime Video and HBO Max.

	The project has institutional backing from Spain’s ICAA and the Málaga Provincial Council, alongside private capital. It also has the support of Spanish soccer club Málaga CF, which has been involved since the start of filming and has agreed to take part in a series of promotional activities around the film’s release.



	

									Paco Torres © Raúl Pérez

title: California Attorney General Slams David Ellison’s Plan to Pull Paramount Out of the State as ‘Blackmail’ Attempt That ‘Won’t Work’
description:
Aug 11, 2026 9:24am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Getty
	

		
	
				
	Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California who is leading a
body:
Aug 11, 2026 9:24am PT	
	

			


			
			
	

									Getty
	

		
	
				
	Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California who is leading a 12-state coalition’s lawsuit seeking to block Paramount’s takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery, responded to David Ellison‘s threat to pull Paramount out of the state unless Bonta agrees to settlement talks.

	“In a span of weeks, Paramount agreed to halt the merger until a court decision or until June 2027, asked for a November trial, and is now back with another attempt to blackmail the state into letting an illegal deal through,” Bonta wrote in a post on X.
	

	Bonta continued, “Paramount has lost the plot as it continues to lose in court. It didn’t work the first time — on the eve of our July lawsuit — and it won’t work this time.”


	Ellison told Paramount senior execs last week that, while he is confident the company will prevail in court against the states’ antitrust lawsuit, he’s prepared to relocate Paramount (as well as Warner Bros. if the merger successfully closes) unless Bonta agrees to negotiate a settlement. Ellison said the company will begin the process of exiting California starting Oct. 1 in the event that such talks have not started, and he told his team the Paramount Skydance board has approved the move.

	More to come


	
		More from Variety

title: Leah Remini Signs With WME (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Leah Remini has signed with WME for representation, Variety has learned exclusively. She continues to be repped by Del Shaw Moonves Tanaka Finkelste
body:
Leah Remini has signed with WME for representation, Variety has learned exclusively. She continues to be repped by Del Shaw Moonves Tanaka Finkelstein & Lezcano. 

	WME will work with Remini to further expand her brand across television, film, digital media, podcasting, original content development, and additional platforms. 

	Remini is best known for her work in front of the camera, including her starring role in the hit sitcom “The King of Queens.” She starred alongside Kevin James in the series for nine seasons between 1998 and 2007 at CBS. The pair reunited in the CBS sitcom “Kevin Can Wait” in 2017. 
	

	Her other acting credits include early appearances on the popular comedy “Who’s The Boss,” which led to the spinoff series “Living Dolls.” She has also been seen in shows like “Cheers,” “Friends,” “NYPD Blue,” and “Saved by the Bell,” as well as films like “Old School” and “Second Act.” 


	Behind the camera, Remini is known for creating, hosting, and executive producing the hit A&E docuseries “Leah Remini: Scientology and the Aftermath” with Mike Rinder. The show received four Emmy nominations during its run, winning two. She and Rinder also created and co-hosted the popular iHeartRadio podcast “Scientology: Fair Game,” while Remini published her memoir, “Troublemaker: Surviving Hollywood and Scientology.”

	She has also starred in unscripted series including “Inside Out: Leah Remini” at VH1 as well as “Leah Remini: It’s All Relative” at TLC. 

	As a host, she was one of the original co-hosts of “The Talk” at CBS and later served as a co-host and guest judge on “Dancing with the Stars,” having also competed on the show. She then hosted and executive produced “People Puzzler” for Game Show Network, which earned her a Daytime Emmy nomination. The same year, she also served as a judge on Fox’s “So You Think You Can Dance.”

title: Isabelle Stever Discusses Challenges of Shooting Locarno Competition Title ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ During War
description: “The reality changed our plans,” explains Ukrainian writer Anna Melikova of her new screenplay “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming.” She is seated next to he
body:
“The reality changed our plans,” explains Ukrainian writer Anna Melikova of her new screenplay “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming.” She is seated next to her wife Isabelle Stever, the director of their new film, at the Locarno Film Festival. Their second creative collaboration after the Berlinale premiering “Grand Jeté” (2022), “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” marks Stever’s long-awaited return to Locarno after her debut “Gisela” played in the Filmmakers of the Present section back in 2005.
	

	“I wanted to write a story about my friends, about their love story,” Melikova continues. And while “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” retains its original shape as a version of this queer love story (with a dash of Melikova and Stever’s own), the screenplay was forced to evolve rather abruptly in 2022 when Russia mounted a full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Melikova’s Berlinale Kompagnon Fellowship Award-winning script was no longer simply about how transition impacts a couple, but how it does when their lives are interrupted by war.




	

									Courtesy of X Filme Creative Pool
	



	On New Year’s Eve, a few months before the invasion, Oleh (Markus Bright) has much to celebrate; he has finally received a passport with his name and gender marker adjusted to male. His long-term girlfriend Olya (Tania Myronyshena) gives him another reason later when she spontaneously proposes: the two can marry now that the state acknowledges them as man and wife. When their excitement for the future is disrupted by Russia’s attacks, the two forge an exit plan that tests the fundamentals of their commitment.

	For the German-Ukrianian pair behind the film, many things did not go according to plan. For practical reasons, Melikova and Stever originally counted on a limited number of days of shooting in Ukraine. “We wanted to film only a few small scenes, all of them outside, with everything else [shot] in Germany.” When they came to Kyiv, looking to cast their paramours, “we felt that we had to film there.” Their reason: authenticity. 
	

	A similar pursuit was reflected in the way the filmmaker-writer duo went about assembling their cast, ensuring that it honored the script. Luck followed intention. Melikova recollects being part of a festival jury at Kyiv in 2026 and asking if anyone knew of a transgender actor who might be right for the film. “In  five minutes, people sent me pictures of Markus. I showed it to Isabelle and felt that we found Oleh.” Olya was found on the phone when, doomscrolling on Instagram, Melikova chanced upon Myronyshena’s picture.

	Oleh and Olya, the central characters of the film, were imagined as people who shared a likeness — evident but not limited to their similar sounding names. “Isabelle had this vision,” Melikova explains. When Bright and Myronyshena appear on screen, the symmetry of their appearances — short haircut, light eyes — overlaps, enlivening the filmmaker’s intent. 

	Such intimacy of gaze, that sees the other only to see themselves better, accounts for the more tender moments in the film. They also feel like a marvel given that both Bright, a transgender man, and Myronyshena, a journalist at the Kyiv Independent, are non-professional actors. “But,” Stever intervenes, “the way they treated each other and respected the other’s safe space transformed the film from timeless to timely.”

	Yet, mounting a project with them at the frontline and a war raging in the background implied tackling multiple safety concerns. The makers protected the actors from pressure, and learnt to keep the camera rolling even as drone sounds threatened to infiltrate their make-believe world. In one early scene, the shoot had to be moved inside when spatters of drones could be heard nearby — not just an interruption to the schedule, but a concern for the safety of the cast and crew. “You cannot be afraid everyday for three months. You have to have energy for tomorrow. You have to work and sleep through the air alarms.”

	“I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” also appears inclined to settle for safety. Despite its impassioned advocacy for an alternative way of life, the film concludes with a seemingly conventional image that pricks with its neatness. It might seem self-defeating but Stever and Melikova maintain that the ending is, in fact, a question. “What happens when you categorize people and leave the space within?” What happens when the world, volatile in its divisiveness, denies the basic dignity that allows people to sleep? They rarely dream.

schema.headline: Isabelle Stever Discusses Challenges of Shooting Locarno Competition Title ‘I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming’ During War

title: ACLU Demands FCC Release Records Pertaining to ABC Early License Renewal, Alleging Agency’s Stated Rationale for Review ‘Does Not Seem Credible’
description: The American Civil Liberties Union submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to the FCC for records pertaining to the agency’s decision
body:
The American Civil Liberties Union submitted a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request to the FCC for records pertaining to the agency’s decision to require Disney’s eight owned-and-operated ABC stations to renew their broadcast licenses early.

	“[T]his Request concerns whether the government is using its authority to illegally retaliate against broadcasters for saying something the government dislikes, and whether it is attempting to chill protected speech,” the ACLU said in the FOIA request, filed Tuesday. “The publicly released information about why the FCC is asking 8 ABC stations to renew their broadcast licenses early does not seem credible in context, and information about the FCC’s true motivations is not available publicly.”
	

	The FCC in April called for the early review of broadcast licenses for ABC’s eight local TV stations. The agency has said that’s related to holding Disney/ABC accountable to a “public interest” standard and that the review is pursuant to an FCC probe into the media company’s DEI practices. ABC and other critics — including former FCC chairs — have blasted the move as aimed at intimidating broadcasters whose news coverage Trump does not like. In addition, the FCC has initiated a formal review of whether “The View” qualifies for an exemption to the agency’s equal-time rules for political candidates.


	In its FOIA request, the ACLU said, “We believe that the FCC’s stated basis for requiring the early license renewal is mere pretext for punishing ABC because the Trump Administration disliked what ABC’s on-air talent had to say. We also believe the FCC and the Trump Administration are trying to send a message to other broadcasters that if they air content the Administration doesn’t like, they could face similar penalties.”
	

	“To provide the American public with information about whether the FCC is using its authority to illegally retaliate against broadcasters’ speech, and attempting to chill protected speech, the ACLU seeks information about the FCC’s motivation for requiring ABC stations to renew their broadcast licenses early through this Request,” the rights organization said in the filing.

	Representatives for the FCC did not respond to a request for comment. ABC declined to comment.

	The FCC’s call for early license renewal came one day after Donald Trump and Melania Trump publicly criticized a joke about Jimmy Kimmel made on his show on April 23 (Kimmel said Melania had “a glow like an expectant widow”). On April 27, Melania Trump posted to X that “Kimmel shouldn’t have the opportunity to enter our homes each evening to spread hate… Enough is enough. It is time for ABC to take a stand.” The same day, Trump wrote on Truth Social that “Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC.” On April 28, the FCC’s Media Bureau issued an order requiring Disney “to file license renewals for all of their licensed TV stations within 30 days.” The station’s licenses were otherwise not due for renewal until between 2028 and 2031.

	“The timing of the order would be suspicious enough on its own – but in context of other recent retaliatory action against ABC, there is little doubt about the FCC’s true goals,” the ACLU asserted in the FOIA filing.

	In response to past criticism of the FCC’s review of ABC’s broadcast licenses, an agency spokesperson said, “As the agency decision makes clear, the early renewal order is based on a long-running FCC investigation into Disney’s DEI conduct, not any speech.” When Carr was asked at an April 30 press conference at the FCC if the Kimmel joke would play a part in the FCC’s review of the ABC licenses, he responded that Disney is “going to have to come in and demonstrate that they’ve been operating in the public interest.”

	The ACLU filing notes that “This isn’t the first time that the Trump FCC threatened regulatory action against ABC over one of Jimmy Kimmel’s jokes.” In September 2026, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr threatened to investigate ABC affiliates unless they took Kimmel’s show off the air (or unless ABC fired Kimmel) after the late-night host made remarks about Charlie Kirk’s murder. Carr said on a podcast, “Look, we can do this the easy way or the hard way… these companies can find ways to … take action on Kimmel or, you know, there’s going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.” In the wake of Carr’s threat, ABC briefly took Kimmel off the air before a public backlash led ABC to reverse course.
	

	The ACLU also alleges that the FCC’s review of “The View’s” equal-time exemption represents “seemingly retaliatory regulatory action against ABC.”

	“The Trump FCC’s abuse of power to investigate, threaten, or regulate other broadcasters after President Trump has taken issue with their coverage also indicates that the FCC required Disney-owned ABC stations to renew their licenses early to punish them for their speech,” the organization said in the FOIA request.

	For example, on May 28 the FCC issued a “reminder” to broadcasters that their licenses were a “privilege” dependent on operating in the public interest, the ACLU noted. “Prior to the ‘reminder,’ the President had repeatedly called for the revocation of broadcast licenses for broadcasters that he thinks cover him unfairly. In fact, Chairman Carr has publicly stated that his interpretation of the public interest standard takes into account a broadcasters’ viewpoint, stating ‘the public interest means you can’t be running a narrow, partisan circus and still meeting your public interest obligations.’”

	“The FCC’s ‘reminder’ ended with a clear threat against those who broadcast content that angers the President — ‘the Commission will not hesitate to exercise its statutory authority to ensure thatbroadcasters either fulfill their public interest obligation or provide the privilege of being abroadcast licensee to someone that will fulfill that duty,’” the ACLU said in the FOIA request.

	The ACLU’s FOIA requests asks for the release of records (including internal and external emails, meeting minutes, legal and policy memoranda, guidance documents, instructions, formal and informal presentations) pertaining to:


The decision to require Disney-owned ABC stations to renew their broadcast licenses early.
All communications to, from, or among FCC employees or commissioners since January 20, 2025 discussing Disney, ABC, a Disney-owned ABC affiliate, any official of Disney or ABC, Jimmy Kimmel, or staff of Jimmy Kimmel Live!.
All communications to, from, or among FCC employees or Commissioners since January 20, 2025 discussing complaints from President Trump, Melania Trump, JD Vance, Usha Vance, Susie Wiles, Dan Scavino, Stephen Miller, James Blair, Taylor Budowich, Vince Haley, David Warrington, Steven Cheung, Karoline Leavitt, Robin Colwell, Paige Willey or Ryan Baasch about what was said during an ABC broadcast or referencing a broadcast license.



	The ACLU concluded its request, “If the Request is denied in whole or in part, the ACLU asks that you justify all deletions by reference to specific exemptions to FOIA. The ACLU expects the release of all segregable portions of otherwise exempt material.”

	A copy of the ACLU’s FOIA request is available at this link.

schema.headline: ACLU Demands FCC Release Records Pertaining to ABC Early License Renewal, Alleging Agency’s Stated Rationale for Review ‘Does Not Seem Credible’

title: ‘Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story’ Trailer: Ella Beatty Is an Axe Murderer in the Fourth Chapter of Ryan Murphy’s Bloody Anthology Series
description: Netflix has released the trailer for “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story,” the fourth chapter in Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s anthology drama series.
body:
Netflix has released the trailer for “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story,” the fourth chapter in Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s anthology drama series. This time around, the subject is Lizzie Borden, a young woman who was accused of hacking her parents to death with an axe in the late 19th century. 

	The official logline for “The Lizzie Borden Story” reads, “When the repressed daughter of a wealthy New England family and her rebellious maid find themselves trapped in a house built on humiliation and cruelty, they escape into a fantasy of sex, power, and revenge. The gruesome unsolved murders that follow don’t just shock the world—they give birth to an icon who refuses to live imprisoned in a cage, choosing instead to forge her own legend: shocking, monstrous, and gloriously free.”
	

	Ella Beatty stars as Borden, a 32-year-old Sunday school teacher who was suspected of murdering her father and mother with an axe in 1893. She was said to have delivered nearly 40 axe blows to both her parents inside the family’s home. Although she was tried for her crimes, the jury acquitted her.


	The eight-episode series features Rebecca Hall as Abby Borden, Lizzie’s stepmother, and Charlie Hunnam as her father, Andrew Borden. Hunman recently received an Emmy nomination for his portrayal of serial killer Ed Gein in the previous season of Murphy’s “Monster” series. 

	Other cast members include Billie Lourd, Joey Pollari, Sarah Paulson and Jessica Barden.

	Murphy co-created “Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story” with Brennan, who also serves as writer. The pair executive produces alongside Max Winkler, Eric Kovtun, Scott Robertson, Louise Shore, Nissa Diederich, Todd Kubrak, Carl Franklin and Tanasa Popa. Winkler and Sarah Adina Smith direct. 
	

	This is Murphy and Brennan’s fourth installment of the “Monster” series, marking the first to focus on a female killer. The previous season followed Jeffrey Dahmer, Ed Gein and the Menendez brothers. 

	The story of Lizzie Borden was previously adapted in Lifetime’s “The Lizzie Borden Chronicles” with Christina Ricci as the titular character, and the 2018 film “Lizzie,” starring Chloë Sevigny as Borden and Kristen Stewart as maid Bridget Sullivan.

	Check out the trailer below.

title: Mateo Ybarra’s ‘Small Talk,’ a Locarno Premiere, Takes a Peek Into Switzerland’s Last Remaining Etiquette School for Women
description:
“Small Talk,” directed my Mateo Ybarra (“Over Our Hills,” “Summer Camp”), will have its world premiere at the Locarno Film Festival on Aug. 11.

	Th
body:
“Small Talk,” directed my Mateo Ybarra (“Over Our Hills,” “Summer Camp”), will have its world premiere at the Locarno Film Festival on Aug. 11.

	The film stars Hélène Bares (“Evy & Me”) as Charlie, who signs up for a summer course at Switzerland’s only remaining etiquette school for women. Her reason for attending is to land a career within the elite luxury industry. The film profiles real women from all over the world and addresses issues of underlying gender roles, class hierarchy, and female empowerment.
	

	“What makes ‘Small Talk’ stand out is the way fiction and documentary truly feed into each other. On one hand you’re emotionally invested in Charlie’s story, on the other you’re watching this fascinating institution with almost an ethnographic curiosity. You leave the film both fully entertained and full of questions about the world, which is pretty rare,” said Garance Targowla, sales & acquisition manager at Urban Sales, which handles “Small Talk.”


	The film is produced by Mateo Ybarra and Madeline Robert of L’Artifice, and co-produced by RTS Radio Télévision Suisse.



	

									Mateo Ybarra
	



	Variety interviewed Mateo Ybarra ahead of its world premiere.

	Which part of the film is documentary and which part is fiction?  

	Mateo Ybarra: It’s the very question that the film asks the audience: in an environment where people learn to perform within high society, who is ultimately playing a role?

	From the very beginning, however, one element was absolutely clear to everyone involved in the process: actress Hélène Bares was invited to take part in the program as a genuine student, attending the full six-week intensive course alongside the other participants.
	

	All of the students are actually taking the course and appear in the film as themselves. The same is true of the teaching staff and the classes themselves.

	How did you come to learn of the school and what motivated you to make a film about it?

	Ybarra: The school has existed for more than 70 years and, although it is now the last finishing school of its kind in Switzerland, it belongs to a tradition that once thrived.

	A friend first told me about it back in 2016, pointing out that Swiss filmmakers rarely film within their own country, despite the wealth of fascinating places and institutions it has to offer. That conversation stayed with me and ultimately led me in this direction.

	Is the school for women only? 

	Ybarra: The school’s main six-week summer program is exclusively for women. Although it offers mixed courses during the rest of the year, its core activity remains primarily for women. They also told me that they have regularly asked students whether they would like to include men in the program, but so far they have preferred to keep it women-only.

	How do you see this institution from a feminist perspective?

	Ybarra: The school belongs to a tradition in which young women were educated to fulfill roles as wives, mothers and hostesses, reflecting gender roles and social norms that are now widely regarded as sexist or outdated. The curiosity surrounding this kind of institution today stems precisely from the question of how such a school can still exist. Yet today, it presents itself as a protected space, free from male presence, whose purpose is to equip women with the tools to navigate a society still largely structured by patriarchal norms.

	If feminism is understood as a movement against all forms of domination and oppression, then I believe there remains an unresolved paradox in attempting to pursue this ideal within a society structured by vertical hierarchies and ultra-capitalist values.

	What interested me was witnessing how people negotiate with the systems that already exist. I wanted to show that they are not necessarily victims of those systems, but are often fully conscious of them. Social change happens more slowly than our political aspirations.

	Charlie seems to evolve dramatically as time goes by.
	

	Ybarra: How Charlie would experience the school remained an open question throughout the shoot. Of course, we imagined several possible directions, depending on how her journey unfolded.

	We built the film around a character who chooses to invest in this program in the hope of achieving a form of social and professional mobility that might allow her to move beyond her current circumstances. Yet the social expectations and the pressure exerted by the world she aspires to join are very real. This raises the question of how one preserves one’s identity, and whether that is ultimately possible at all. 

	How did the real students taking the course feel about being filmed?

	Ybarra: The film relies on a very delicate balance between what we learn through the institute’s classes, Charlie’s personal journey, and, above all, the presence of the other students. What surprised us most was the extraordinary ability of the students to embrace the cinematic proposition. We gradually realized that many of them had spent their lives navigating complex social expectations, and that this experience had given them an exceptional ease in front of the camera. 

	Their generosity, freedom and sincerity moved us deeply. They are not simply people being filmed; they became essential presences within the narrative, giving the film a truth and vitality that we could never have written ourselves. Reality is such wonderful material.

title: RioFilme to Announce New Incentives for International Co-Productions, Unveiling Them at Brazil’s Gramado Fest (EXCLUSIVE)
description: RioFilme, the film-TV agency of Rio de Janeiro City, will launch a call for proposals amounting to R$15 million ($3 million) for up to four internat
body:
RioFilme, the film-TV agency of Rio de Janeiro City, will launch a call for proposals amounting to R$15 million ($3 million) for up to four international co-production projects involving Rio-based companies.

	Leonardo Edde, president of RioFilme, told Variety that projects of fiction and animated feature films are eligible to apply and that he will provide details of the new funding line during his Gramado Film Market panel at the Gramado Fest 2026.
	

	In order to apply, a project must abide by Brazilian regulations. If the co-production partner of the Rio-based company is from one of the 13 countries that has coproduction agreements with Brazil – South Africa, Germany, Argentina, Canada, Chile, Spain, France, India, Israel, Italy, Portugal, the UK and Venezuela – the co-production conditions must be within the agreements’ rules.


	If not, the Rio partner must share of at least 40 of the film’s rights and two-thirds of the artists and technicians in the production should be Brazilians, as determined in the general co-production rules of Brazil’s National Cinema Agency (Ancine).

	Edde said the new funding line is just part of an ambitious plan to further consolidate Rio as a major world film and TV production hub. Over the past years, Rio has streamlined its film commission and created incentives that made it one of the most filmed cities in the world, surpassing Paris and Mexico City in terms of days shot in the city. In the first half of 2026, Rio hosted 40 international productions, up from 28 in the same period last year, according to Rio Filme.
	

	The next step to Rio is to foster relations with China, Russia and India, partners of Brazil in the Brics alliance, but currently with residual cooperation in film and TV, said Edde.

	“The Brics project has still not taken off in a manner commensurate with its potential. I believe the integration between the countries will be achieved through the cultural industry, especially the audiovisual industry,” he said. “There is a Brics film festival from time to time, and there are some other initiatives, but they are unfortunately not yet permanent, recurring or a priority for the countries.”

	The main target is China. The countries are celebrating this year the Brazil–China Cultural Year 2026 and the Brazilian Congress is about to approve a co-production agreement between the two nations.

	Brazil’s Ministry of Culture sent in June a large delegation of government officials, industry representatives and talents to the 28th Shanghai International Film Festival, Edde included, and organized screenings of Brazilian films in eight Chinese cities.

	During the trip, Edde advanced on plans for a visit of members of the China Film Producers’ Association (CFPA) to Rio de Janeiro over Nov. 16-19. He has also initiated the process to enroll RioFilm in the UHD World Association (UWA), a technical and industrial organization with nearly 500 company members, such as giants Huawei, iQIYI, Baidu, Alibaba, and Xiaomi.

	According to Edde, RioFilme is negotiating a partnership with the Hengdian Group, owner of the Hengdian World Studios, located in Zhejiang Province, the world’s largest film and television production center. 

	The complex includes numerous large-scale studios, outdoor sets and replicas of Chinese cities, palaces and historical landmarks of China, as well as crews with equipment, costumes, props, accommodation, technicians and supporting actors. It is also a major tourist destination.

	The idea is to have Hengdian as the model for Rio’s Creative District, which includes the main sports complex of the Rio 2016 Summer Olympics, the city’s Cinema Pole that will have 16 studios by the end of this year and the production centers of free-to-air TV networks Globo and Record.

	As for Russia, RioFilme and the Moscow Film Cluster (Moskino) signed a partnership agreement during Moscow International Film Week 2025. Moskino sent in May 2026 a large delegation to Rio2C, the big creative industry meeting in Rio de Janeiro. In addition, the two countries are negotiating a coproduction agreement.
	

	India is also on RioFilme’s radar. Daniel Celli, coordinator of the Rio Film Commission, attended over Aug. 6-7 the first edition of the Brics Waves Bazaar, held in Mumbai, which gathered producers, studio and streaming executives, investors, government agencies and media-technology companies from Brics countries.

	“India and Brazil both have a great film tradition,” Edde said. “We have been discussing with Indian officials how some form of financing could be created to dub and license Brazilian and Indian content. The idea is to make them available on open-access streaming platforms.” 



	

					Leonardo Edde at the Moscow International Film Week 2025

schema.headline: RioFilme to Announce New Incentives for International Co-Productions, Unveiling Them at Brazil’s Gramado Fest (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Taylor Swift Named to the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, Becoming Its Youngest Inductee Ever
description: Taylor Swift will be adding another trophy to her shelf, as the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame announced Tuesday that the superstar will be indu
body:
Taylor Swift will be adding another trophy to her shelf, as the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame announced Tuesday that the superstar will be inducted into the hall this fall, becoming, at 36, the youngest writer ever to receive the honor.

	Swift sent a message to be read by Mark Ford, executive director of the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, as he announced this year’s inductees in a livestream.


	“From the time I started writing songs as a child, I fixated on Nashville as the perfect place to be,” said Swift in her statement. “I wanted to learn with and from the best and get to immerse myself in a community of storytellers, and thankfully Nashville turned out to be exactly what I’d dreamed of. A town that validated and prioritized hard work, determination and imagination. Where the writers show up to work every day even when the mysterious muses and the magic don’t. To be honored by this city I love so much is a beautiful thing, and I’m very grateful.”
	

	The accolade follows on the heels of Swift having been inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in New York in June, at which point she became the youngest female writer ever to join that hall.

	Swift was inducted into the Nashville hall in a category that honors songwriters that have been at it for 20 years or longer, in what, not coincidentally, is the 20th anniversary year for her debut album, “Taylor Swift.”

	Also named to the hall as part of Tuesday’s announcement: Lyle Lovett, Shawn Camp, Lee Thomas Miller and Bruce Channel.

	“I’m so happy that Taylor Swift finally got a break,” quipped Miller, stepping to the podium at the announcement event to thank the hall. “She needed a win.”
	

	Swift was elected in the contemporary songwriter/artist category, while Camp and Miller got in in the contemporary songwriter category, Channel in the veteran songwriter category, and Lovett in the veteran songwriter/artist division.

	A list of credits probably isn’t necessary for Swift and Lovett, who write or co-write all of their material as recording artists. Camp also has renown as an artist, though he has enjoyed cuts with many hitmakers, including Garth Brooks’ Two Piña Coladas,” Willie Nelson’s “A Beautiful Time” and Brooks & Dunn’s “How Long Gone.” Miller’s credits include the Jamey Johnson hit “In Color,” Joe Nichols’ “The Impossible” and Trace Adkins’ “You’re Gonna Miss This.” Channel’s list of recorded hits includes the self-recorded “Hey! Baby!,” Mel McDaniel’s “Stand Up” and John Conlee’s “As Long as I’m Rockin’ With You.” 

	Other nominees this year included Chris Stapleton, Miranda Lambert, Phil Vassar, Jim Beavers, Rodney Clawson, Dallas Davidson, Marv Green, Neil Thrasher and Chris Tompkins.

	The hall was established in 1970 and had 254 members prior to this announcement. Last year’s inductees were Emmylou Harris, Brad Paisley, Jim Lauderdale, JJ Cale, Steve Bogard, Don Cook and Tony Martin.

	The induction ceremony will take place at a yet-to-be-specified date this fall, Ford said.

            A child's playtime inside a Kansas home turned deadly ... when a 4-year-old was allegedly electrocuted by a clothes dryer.
      
    
            The Allen County Sheriff's Office says the child was playing at a residence in Savonburg on Thursday when they reportedly received an electrical shock from a 220-volt dryer.
      
    
            Deputies responded to a report of a child not breathing shortly after 9:30 PM ... but by then, the parents were already racing their unconscious child to Neosho Memorial Regional Medical Center in Chanute.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The child was later declared dead at the hospital.
      
    
            Law enforcement says they are investigating ... but "no foul play is suspected at this time, and it appears to have been a tragic accident."
      
    
            The child's identity has not been released ... ditto for the parents.

            Gloria was 91.
